title: Natural and made materials: how sand becomes glass

summary.text: A glass bangle is clear, but the sand it was made from is not. Some materials, like wood, cotton, clay and sand, come from nature. Others, like glass, paper and plastic, are made by people from natural materials. In this unit you watch white sugar grains turn into a clear sheet, the way sand turns into glass. You also find out how paper comes from plants and plastic from oil, and you bury some materials in soil to see which ones break down.
summary.art: A heap of pale sand beside a clear glass bangle, a log beside a notebook, and a drop of black oil beside a plastic bucket, joined by arrows.

intro.hook: Hold a glass tumbler up to the window. You can see right through it. Glass is made from sand. Now pour a little sand or salt into your hand. Can you see through the heap?
intro.text: You cannot see through a heap of sand. Yet a glass window, made from sand, is clear. How can that be? People change natural materials to make new ones. They melt sand to make glass. They mash wood to make paper. They make plastic from oil that comes from deep under the ground. Before you read on, guess. What do people do to sand to make it clear? You are going to find out, with sugar instead of sand.
intro.art: A child holding a clear glass tumbler up to a window in one hand, and a small heap of pale sand in the other palm.

outcomes: By the end I can sort things into natural materials and materials made by people.
By the end I can say which natural material glass, paper and plastic are each made from.
By the end I can say how heat changes sand into glass, from what I saw in the sugar test.
By the end I can explain why a heap of grains looks white, but one melted piece is clear.
By the end I can say which materials break down in soil, from my soil cup test.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: A material that comes from nature: from plants, from animals or from the ground.
terms.example: Wood, cotton, wool, clay, stone and sand are natural materials.
terms.art: A log, a cotton boll, a ball of wool and a heap of sand in a row.

terms.meaning: A material that people make by changing natural materials. People also call it a man-made material.
terms.example: Glass, paper, plastic, steel and brick are made materials.
terms.art: A glass bottle, a notebook, a plastic bucket and a brick in a row.

terms.meaning: The natural material that something is made from.
terms.example: Sand is the raw material for glass. Wood is a raw material for paper.
terms.art: An arrow from a heap of sand to a glass bottle.

terms.meaning: To turn from a solid into a liquid by heating.
terms.example: Sand melts in a very hot furnace. Ghee melts in a warm pan.
terms.art: A spoon of hard ghee turning runny in a warm pan.

terms.meaning: A very hot oven used to melt things, such as sand or metal.
terms.example: Glass furnaces in Firozabad, in Uttar Pradesh, melt glass to make bangles.
terms.art: A glowing orange furnace with a worker holding a long metal rod at its mouth.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. Paper is made of tiny plant fibres pressed together.
terms.example: Tear a tissue slowly, and you can see little fibres at the torn edge.
terms.art: A torn edge of tissue paper, with a zoom-in circle showing tiny threads.

terms.meaning: Lets light through so well that you can see clearly through it.
terms.example: Clear glass and clean water are transparent.
terms.art: A child reading a word through a clear glass tumbler.

terms.meaning: To slowly fall apart into tiny pieces, often because tiny living beings eat the material.
terms.example: A banana peel in soil breaks down in a few weeks. A plastic bag takes far longer.
terms.art: A banana peel going from yellow, to brown, to black and crumbly in soil.

explanations.context: This card explains what a natural material is.
explanations.definition: A natural material is found in nature. It comes from plants, from animals or from the ground.
explanations.description: Wood and cotton grow on plants. Wool grows on sheep, and silk is spun by silkworms, who are the caterpillars of a moth. Clay, sand, stone and the rocks that metals come from are dug out of the ground. People may cut or clean a natural material, but it stays the same material. A wooden plank is still wood.
examples: From plants: wood, cotton, jute, coir from coconuts, bamboo.
From the ground: clay, sand, stone, salt.
explanations.art: Three groups: a tree and a cotton plant, a sheep and a silkworm cocoon, and a heap of clay and sand.

explanations.context: This card explains what a made material is, and where its raw material comes from.
explanations.definition: A made material is made by people, by changing one or more natural materials so much that they become a new material.
explanations.description: People never start from nothing. Every made material begins as a natural raw material. Glass begins as sand. Paper begins as wood or other plant parts. Plastic begins as oil and gas from deep under the ground. Brick begins as clay. The raw material is changed by heating, mashing or mixing, and a new material comes out.
examples: Wood, bamboo or sugarcane waste becomes paper.
Clay becomes brick when it is baked.
explanations.art: Four arrows: sand to a bottle, a tree to a notebook, an oil drop to a bucket, a lump of clay to a brick.

explanations.concept: How glass is made from sand
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the sugar test: why the melted sugar was clear, and how sand becomes glass in the same way.
explanations.definition: Glass is made by melting sand with a little soda and limestone in a furnace, then letting it cool into a hard, clear solid.
explanations.description: Each grain of glass-making sand is a tiny clear piece. A heap of grains looks pale and you cannot see through it, because light bounces off the edges of every grain. In a furnace at about 1,500 degrees Celsius, the grains melt into one thick, glowing liquid. Now there are no edges inside, so light goes straight through. Workers blow, press or pull the hot glass into bottles, windows and bangles. As it cools, it goes hard. The melted sugar did the same thing. It was white as grains, and clear as one piece.
examples: Bangles from Firozabad are made of melted glass, pulled and coiled while hot.
Old glass bottles are crushed and melted again to make new ones.
Crushed glass looks white, like sugar, because it has many edges again.
explanations.art: Three pictures: a heap of sand, a glowing orange blob of melted glass on a rod, and a clear glass bottle.

explanations.concept: How paper is made from plants
explanations.context: This card explains how paper is made, and what you saw in the water shake.
explanations.definition: Paper is made by mashing plant parts in water until they come apart into tiny fibres, then spreading the fibres thin, pressing them and drying them.
explanations.description: Most paper is made from wood. In India, a lot of paper is also made from bamboo and from bagasse. Bagasse is what is left of sugarcane after the juice is squeezed out. In a paper mill, the plant parts are cooked and beaten in water into a soft mush called pulp. The pulp is spread on a fine screen, and the water drains away. The fibres dry and hold on to each other, and that makes a sheet. When paper gets very wet, the fibres let go again. That is why your tissue fell apart in the water shake.
examples: A paper mill in Karur, Tamil Nadu, makes paper from sugarcane bagasse.
Notebooks, newspapers, paper bags and tissues are all plant fibres.
Old paper can be mashed in water and made into new paper.
explanations.art: A tree trunk, then a tub of soft grey pulp, then a sheet of wet pulp on a screen, then a stack of paper.

explanations.concept: How plastic is made from oil
explanations.context: This card explains where plastic comes from, and why it did not change in the soil cup test.
explanations.definition: Most plastic is made in factories from oil and natural gas, which are dug out from deep under the ground.
explanations.description: Oil formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny living beings that lived in the sea. In a factory, very small particles from oil are joined into very long chains. Those chains make plastic. Plastic is melted and pressed into buckets, bottles and bags. The bacteria and fungi in soil eat banana peel and paper easily. They have very few ways to eat plastic, so plastic can stay in soil for a very long time. Scientists have found a few bacteria that can eat some kinds of plastic, but only slowly.
examples: Buckets, mugs, toothbrushes and milk packets are plastic.
Polyester cloth in many clothes is a plastic too.
In the soil cup test, the plastic bag looked the same after two weeks.
explanations.art: A drop of black oil deep under the ground, then a factory, then a plastic bucket and a bottle.

explanations.concept: Where is the line between natural and made?
explanations.context: This card is about the hard cases, where people do not agree whether a material is natural or made.
explanations.description: Easy cases are easy. A stone is natural and a plastic mug is made by people. But think of a cotton shirt. Cotton is natural, yet people spun it into thread and wove it into cloth. A paper wasp chews wood and makes real paper for her nest. A bird weaves a nest from grass. People answer these cases in different ways.
examples: A cotton shirt: natural fibre, made by people into cloth.
A wasp's paper nest: paper made by an animal.
A brick: clay, baked so hot that it can never turn back into clay.

perspectives.explanation: If the material is still the same stuff, like cotton in a shirt or wood in a chair, it is natural. If it has become a new material, like glass or plastic, it is made.
Humans are animals. If a wasp's paper is natural, then our paper is natural too. Animals, including us, change natural materials all the time.
The question that matters most is whether the material can break down and go back into the soil. Banana leaves can. Most plastic cannot, for a very long time.

explanations.art: A cotton shirt, a paper wasp nest and a bird's nest, with a question mark over each.

agreed.text: Glass is made by melting sand, and it is clear because, once melted, it has no grain edges inside to bounce the light about.
agreed.evidence: Glass makers have melted sand into glass for more than 4,000 years. Crush clear glass into powder, and the powder looks white, because it has many edges again.

agreed.text: Paper is a sheet of tiny plant fibres holding on to each other.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, paper looks like a flat mat of thin threads. Soak it and shake it, and the threads come apart.

agreed.text: Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas, and it takes a very long time to break down.
agreed.evidence: Plastic factories use oil and gas as their raw materials. In soil tests, plastic looks the same after months, while peel and paper break down.

challenging.claim: Glass is really a liquid that flows very slowly. That is why old church windows are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.for: Glass has no neat rows of particles inside, like a liquid. Some very old windows really are thicker at one edge.
challenging.against: Old glass was made in uneven sheets, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Some old windows have the thick edge at the top or the side. Scientists worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow enough to see.
challenging.context: This card is about a story many people tell about glass.

challenging.claim: Plastic has nothing natural in it.
challenging.for: Plastic is made in factories, and nothing like a plastic bucket grows in nature.
challenging.against: Plastic is made from oil, and oil formed from tiny sea living beings long ago. The very first plastics, in the 1860s, were made from cotton. Every made material starts as a natural one.
challenging.context: This card is about where plastic comes from.

challenging.claim: Natural materials are always better than made ones.
challenging.for: Many natural materials, like banana leaves, cotton and clay, break down in soil and go back to the earth. Plastic stays for a very long time.
challenging.against: Some made materials do jobs that natural ones cannot. Glass lets light in and keeps the rain out. Steel holds up bridges. And some natural materials are harmful, like poisonous plants. Which is better depends on the job and on what happens to it afterwards.
challenging.context: This card is about whether natural or made materials are better.

big_questions.q: Why was the heap of sugar white, but the melted sheet clear?
big_questions.hint: Think of light bouncing off the edges of every little grain.

big_questions.q: If you crushed a clear glass bangle into powder, what colour would the powder be? Why?
big_questions.hint: Remember what happened when you crushed a piece of your sugar sheet.

big_questions.q: Is a bird's nest natural or made?
big_questions.hint: A bird made it from grass. People make paper from wood. What is the difference?

big_questions.q: When a glass bangle breaks and is thrown away, will it ever become sand again?
big_questions.hint: Think of waves rolling broken glass on a beach for many years.

big_questions.q: Is anything in your home not made from something natural?
big_questions.hint: Pick any thing and follow it back. What was it before?

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,000 years ago, a Roman writer named Pliny the Elder told a story about how glass was first made. Some sailors, he said, landed on a sandy beach and cooked their food. They had no stones for their pot, so they rested it on lumps of soda from their cargo. In the heat of the fire, the soda and the sand melted together, and a stream of clear glass ran out. For a long time many people believed this story. But glass makers today know that a cooking fire is not hot enough to melt sand into glass. It needs a closed furnace, much hotter than any open fire. Archaeologists have found that people in West Asia were making glass beads more than 4,000 years ago. In India, glass makers at Arikamedu, near Puducherry, made tiny glass beads that travelled across Asia and Africa. The American archaeologist Vimala Begley, working with the Indian archaeologist K. V. Raman, dug at Arikamedu from 1989 to 1992. Her team showed that the bead making there began more than 2,000 years ago.
how_we_found_out.who: Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer; the glass bead makers of Arikamedu; Vimala Begley and K. V. Raman, archaeologists
how_we_found_out.when: Glass beads in West Asia more than 4,000 years ago; Pliny's story about 2,000 years ago; digs at Arikamedu, 1989 to 1992
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That glass was first made by chance on a beach, when sailors' cooking fire melted sand and soda. A cooking fire is not hot enough. Glass needs a closed furnace, which is why early glass was made by skilled workers in workshops.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman archaeologist kneeling in a dig near the sea, holding up a tiny blue glass bead between two fingers, with a tray of beads beside her.

story.title: The Green Stone That Was Not a Stone
story.note: Sea glass is real: broken glass rolled by waves and sand for years becomes smooth and frosted. Wet sea glass looks clearer, because water fills the tiny scratches for a while. Nila, Arun and their mother are made up.
text: Nila was seven. She lived in Puducherry, near the sea. Every Sunday morning, before the sun got hot, she walked on the beach with her mother and her little brother Arun.
Arun was five. He liked to collect shells. Nila liked to collect anything that looked strange.
One Sunday, near the line of wet sand, Nila saw something green. She picked it up. It was smooth and flat, with soft round edges. It was cloudy, like a piece of green ice.
"Amma, I found a green stone," she said.
Her mother turned it over in her hand. "That is not a stone," she said. "That is glass."
"It can't be glass," said Arun. "Glass is clear. You can see through glass. And glass is sharp."

"This was once part of a bottle," said Amma. "Maybe someone broke it, a long time ago. The waves rolled it in the sand, back and forth, for years and years. The sand rubbed off the sharp edges. It also made tiny scratches all over it. That is why it looks cloudy now."
Nila held it up to the sun. Light came through, but she could not see the sky through it. Only a soft green glow.
"How did the bottle get to be glass in the first place?" she asked.
Amma smiled. She bent down and picked up a handful of sand. "From this," she said.
Arun laughed. "Sand is not clear. Sand is brown and white. You can't see through sand."

"That's true," said Amma. "You can't see through a heap of sand. But glass makers put sand in a very hot oven called a furnace. The sand melts into a glowing, runny liquid, like thick honey. They blow it into bottles or pull it into bangles. When it cools, it is clear glass."
"But why does it go clear?" asked Nila.
"Look closely at one grain," said Amma. She put a few grains on her dark dupatta. Nila bent close. Some of the grains were tiny, glassy and clear, like little crumbs of glass.

"Each grain lets light through," said Amma. "But in a heap, there are thousands of grains. The light bounces off all their edges, this way and that. So the heap looks pale, and you can't see through it. When the sand melts, all the grains join into one piece. There are no edges left inside. The light goes straight through."
Nila looked at her green glass. "And the scratches on this one are like edges again," she said slowly. "So the light bounces about, and it is cloudy."
"Yes," said Amma. "Now try this."
She took Nila's hand and dipped the glass into a small pool left by a wave. Nila lifted it out, wet and shining.
Now she could see through it. The sky looked green. Arun's face looked green. Even the clouds were green.
"It's clear again!" she said. "The water filled the scratches!"
"The water makes the surface smooth for a moment," said Amma. "When it dries, it will be cloudy again."
Arun took the glass and looked at Nila through it. "So glass is just sand that melted," he said.
"Sand that people melted," said Nila. "The sand came from nature. The glass was made by people. And now the sea is rubbing it back into sand."
Arun thought about this. "Then is it natural or not?" he asked.
Nila did not know. Amma did not say. They walked home with the green glass in Nila's pocket, and Arun's question still in the air.
story.epiphany: A heap of sand is not see-through because light bounces off the edges of all its grains. Melted into one piece, with no edges inside, the same sand becomes clear glass.
ask: Why was Nila's sea glass cloudy?
Why did it go clear when it was wet?
What do you think: is sea glass natural or made by people?
art: A girl on a beach in Puducherry holding up a frosted green piece of glass to the morning sun, her younger brother beside her with a handful of shells.
A mother pointing at a few clear grains of sand on her dark dupatta while the girl bends close.
The girl looking through a wet, shining green glass, with her brother's face tinted green on the other side.

experiments.title: The Sugar Test: can heat turn white grains into a clear sheet?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it onto an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar. Glass is made from sand in the same way, but sand needs a furnace far hotter than a kitchen stove.
experiments.question: White sugar grains are not see-through. If we melt them and let them cool, what will they look like?
experiments.predict: Look at the heap of white sugar. When it is melted and cooled, will it be white, clear, or something else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We keep one spoon of dry sugar aside, not heated, so we can compare. We put the heap of dry sugar and the cooled sugar sheet on the same newspaper, over words of the same size. We count how many letters we can read through each one.

materials.item: white sugar
water
a small steel pan or kadai, and a stove
a steel plate, rubbed with a few drops of cooking oil
a small bowl of cold water, to test if the syrup is ready
a sheet of newspaper
a clean cloth and a steel spoon

experiments.safety: Melted sugar is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Only a grown-up heats and pours it. Children stand at least an arm's length from the stove. Do not touch the sheet until it has cooled for 10 minutes. Soak the pan in water to clean it.

schedule.what: Look at the sugar and guess. A grown-up melts and pours it. Wait for it to cool. Compare the sheet with dry sugar on a newspaper. Crush a piece and look again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the dry heap and the sheet side by side, on top of the newspaper words. Write one sentence: what heat did to the sugar.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Can I read words through it?

setup.art: A spoon of white sugar in a heap on a newspaper, hiding the words under it.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a heap of sugar on the newspaper. Can you see the words?

setup.art: A grown-up stirring bubbling, pale gold syrup in a small steel pan on a stove, with a child watching from a safe distance.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up melts the sugar with a little water.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring golden syrup onto an oiled steel plate, where it spreads into a thin pool.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up pours it onto an oiled plate. Wait 10 minutes.

setup.art: A thin, clear, pale gold sheet of sugar lying on a newspaper, with the printed words easy to read through it, beside a white heap of dry sugar.
setup.caption: 4. Put the cool sheet on the newspaper. Can you see the words now?

flow.do: 1. Put one spoon of dry sugar in a heap on a newspaper word. 2. Let your child look closely. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Can you read the word under the sugar? Now, if I melt this sugar and let it cool, what will it look like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the sugar heap. Can you see the word under it? What will melted sugar look like? Why?

ask.q: What will the melted sugar look like when it cools?
good: White again, because sugar is white.
Clear, like a sweet.
Brown, because it might burn.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Don't correct it. Many children think it will still be white, because they have only seen sugar as white grains.

flow.do: 1. Put 4 tablespoons of sugar and 2 tablespoons of water in the pan. 2. Heat on a medium flame. 3. Stir until the sugar is gone, then stop stirring. 4. Let it bubble for about 6 to 10 minutes.
flow.say: Stay back where you are. Watch the bubbles. Tell me when they change.
flow.kid: Stand back from the stove. Watch the bubbles. Do they change?
flow.parent: After a few minutes the bubbles get smaller and slower, and the syrup turns pale gold. Drop a little into the cold water. If it goes hard and snaps, it is ready. If it bends like chewing gum, heat one or two minutes more. Take it off before it turns dark brown.

flow.do: 1. Pour the syrup slowly onto the oiled steel plate. 2. Tilt the plate a little so it spreads thin. 3. Put the plate somewhere safe to cool.
flow.say: I am pouring it now. Don't touch it. It is hotter than boiling water.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours it. Don't touch. It is very hot.
flow.parent: A thin layer, about as thick as a coin, gives the clearest sheet.

flow.do: 1. Set a timer for 10 minutes. 2. While you wait, look at a few dry grains of sugar on a dark cloth or paper, close up. 3. After 10 minutes, tap the sheet with a spoon to check it is hard.
flow.say: While it cools, look at just a few grains close up. What does one grain look like? Is it white, or can you see light through it?
flow.kid: Look at a few sugar grains up close. Is one grain white? Or is it clear?

ask.q: What does one grain look like up close?
good: It is shiny and clear, like a tiny piece of glass.
It is a little box shape and light comes through.

flow.parent: Under a torch or a phone's camera zoom, single sugar grains look clear and glassy. Only the heap looks white.

flow.do: 1. Lift the cool sheet off the plate. 2. Lay it on a newspaper word next to the dry heap. 3. Count the letters you can read through each. 4. Wrap a small piece in a cloth and tap it with a spoon until it is powder. 5. Look at the powder.
flow.say: How many letters can you read through the heap? Through the sheet? Now, what colour is the crushed sheet? Why do you think it changed?
flow.kid: Count the letters you can read through each one. Now crush a small piece. What colour is it now?

ask.q: Why is the crushed sugar white again?
good: Because it is grains again.
The light bounces off all the little pieces.
It has edges again, so we can't see through.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what your child saw: 'The sheet let me read the word, but the crushed bits did not.' Now read the card 'How glass is made from sand'. You can eat a small piece of the sugar sheet. Break it in the cloth, as edges can be sharp.

check.q: Fathima, a girl in Class 2, crushes a clear glass marble into powder. What colour will the powder look?
check.why: In the sugar test, the clear sheet turned white when it was crushed. Light bounces off the edges of all the tiny bits. Crushed glass looks white for the same reason.

experiments.title: The Soil Cup Test: which materials break down?
experiments.context: In this experiment you bury small pieces of four materials in damp soil. Two are natural and two are made by people. You dig them up after one week and after two weeks to see which ones have started to break down.
experiments.question: Which materials break down in damp soil in two weeks: banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth or a plastic bag?
experiments.predict: Which piece do you think will change the most in two weeks? Which will change the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is about the size of a matchbox. Each one goes in its own cup, under the same amount of soil from the same pot. We give every cup the same 2 spoons of water every two days, and keep them all in the same place.

materials.item: 4 old cups, katoris or cut-off plastic bottles
soil from a potted plant, or a little potting soil
pieces about the size of a matchbox of: banana peel, newspaper, old cotton cloth, a plastic carry bag
a spoon and water
paper labels and sticky tape

experiments.safety: Mould may grow on the peel. Dig with a spoon, don't sniff it, and wash hands with soap afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess. Bury one piece in each cup, label the cups, and water them.
Add 2 spoons of water to each cup.
Dig each piece up with a spoon, look, write what you see, and bury it again.
Add 2 spoons of water to each cup.
Dig up each piece. Compare them. Which changed the most? Sort them: broke down, changed a little, did not change.

experiments.record: Draw each piece on day 1, day 7 and day 14. Write 'natural' or 'made' under each.

setup.art: Four small cups of soil in a row on a windowsill, each with a paper label: peel, newspaper, cloth, plastic.
setup.caption: 1. Bury one piece in each cup. Label the cups.

setup.art: A child adding two spoons of water to a cup of soil.
setup.caption: 2. Water each cup every two days.

setup.art: Four pieces dug up and laid on a newspaper: a black, crumbly banana peel, a soft torn newspaper piece, a stained cloth and an unchanged plastic piece.
setup.caption: 3. After 1 week and 2 weeks, dig them up and look.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the four pieces. 2. Ask which are natural and which are made by people. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which of these come from nature, and which did people make? Which one will change most in the soil? Why?
flow.kid: Which pieces are natural? Which are made? Which will change most? Why?

good: The banana peel, because peels go rotten.
The paper, because it gets soggy.
The plastic will not change, because plastic lasts.

flow.parent: Newspaper is a made material, but it is made of plant fibres. That makes it an interesting one to watch.

flow.do: 1. Fill each cup half full of soil. 2. Lay one piece in each. 3. Cover it with more soil. 4. Add 2 spoons of water. 5. Label each cup.
flow.say: Push the soil down gently. Now each piece is in the dark, in damp soil.
flow.kid: Put one piece in each cup. Cover it with soil. Give it 2 spoons of water.
flow.parent: Keep the cups on a windowsill or a balcony, out of heavy rain. Damp soil works best, not soaking wet.

flow.wait: Leave the cups for 7 days. Water them every 2 days.
flow.do: 1. Dig each piece up with a spoon. 2. Put it on a newspaper and look. 3. Write what you see. 4. Bury it again.
flow.say: What has changed? Look at the colour, and feel how soft it is with the spoon.
flow.kid: Dig up each piece with a spoon. What has changed?

good: The banana peel. It is dark and soft.
The plastic looks the same.

flow.parent: Bacteria and fungi, tiny living beings in the soil, are eating the peel. They break it down.

flow.wait: Leave the cups for another 7 days.
flow.do: 1. Dig up all four pieces. 2. Lay them in a row. 3. Sort them into three groups: broke down, changed a little, did not change. 4. Wash hands with soap.
flow.say: Which pieces have started to break down? Which are natural, and which were made by people? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Sort them: broke down, changed a little, did not change. Was your guess right?

good: The tiny living beings in the soil can't eat it easily.
Plastic is made from oil, and soil bacteria have few ways to eat it.

flow.parent: Cotton takes months to break down, so it may only look stained or a little weaker. That is a real result too. Then read the card 'How plastic is made from oil'.

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Madurai, buries a banana leaf and a plastic plate in soil. After two weeks, which will have changed more?
check.why: In the soil cup test, the banana peel turned soft and black, but the plastic bag did not change. Bacteria and fungi in the soil eat plant materials easily, and plastic only very slowly.

activities.title: The Changing Line: how much did people change it?
activities.context: In this activity you collect things from home and lay them on a line on the floor. At one end go things just as nature made them. At the other end go things that people changed a lot.

materials.item: two sheets of paper: one says 'As nature made it', one says 'Changed a lot by people'
a string, a dupatta or a line of chalk on the floor
8 things from home, for example a banana, a stone or shell, a wooden spoon, a cotton hanky, a clay diya, a notebook, a glass tumbler, a plastic bottle

schedule.what: Collect 8 things. Put each one on the line. Count how many are nearer each end.

activities.record: Draw the line in your notebook with all 8 things on it, in order.

setup.art: A dupatta laid in a straight line on a floor, with a paper at one end reading 'As nature made it' and at the other 'Changed a lot by people'.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the line and the two signs.

setup.art: A banana and a shell at one end of the line, a wooden spoon and a clay diya in the middle, and a glass tumbler and a plastic bottle at the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Put each thing where you think it belongs.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string or dupatta on the floor. 2. Put a sign at each end. 3. Collect 8 things with your child.
flow.say: Let's find 8 things. Find some that came straight from nature, and some that people made.
flow.kid: Find 8 things. Some from nature. Some made by people.
flow.parent: Try to include one of each: something living or grown, something from the ground, something cut from wood, and some glass, paper and plastic.

flow.do: 1. Pick up one thing at a time. 2. Ask your child where it goes on the line, and why. 3. Let them move things as they change their minds.
flow.say: Where does the wooden spoon go? It is still wood, but someone carved it. How much did people change it?
flow.kid: Put each thing on the line. How much did people change it?

ask.q: Why did you put the glass tumbler near the end?
good: Because sand had to be melted to make glass.
You can't find a glass tumbler in nature.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer for the middle things. The reasons matter more than the places.

flow.do: 1. Count the things in the half nearer 'As nature made it'. 2. Count the things in the other half.
flow.say: How many things are on the nature side? How many on the people side? Which side has more?
flow.kid: Count each half. Which half has more things?

check.q: Gurpreet, a girl in Class 2, has a cotton hanky and a plastic bottle. Which one goes nearer the 'Changed a lot by people' end?
check.why: Cotton cloth is still cotton, spun and woven. A plastic bottle is a new material, made from oil in a factory. So people changed the bottle more.

activities.title: Grains Up Close: is one grain white?
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at single grains of sugar and salt on dark paper. You find out whether one grain is white, or only the heap.

materials.item: a pinch of sugar and a pinch of salt
a sheet of dark paper or a dark cloth
a torch, or a phone with a camera that can zoom
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Sprinkle a few grains on dark paper. Shine a torch. Look at one grain, then at a heap.

activities.record: Draw one grain big, and a heap small. Colour them as you saw them.

setup.art: A few sugar grains scattered on black paper, lit by a torch from the side, each grain sparkling like a tiny clear crystal.
setup.caption: 1. Sprinkle a few grains on dark paper. Shine a torch.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a big zoomed-in picture of one clear sugar grain, shaped like a small box.
setup.caption: 2. Look at one grain up close.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a few grains of sugar on the dark paper, spread apart. 2. Shine the torch from the side. 3. Look with a magnifying glass or zoom in with the phone camera.
flow.say: Look at just one grain. What colour is it? Can you see light inside it?
flow.kid: Look at one grain. What colour is it? Can you see light inside?

ask.q: What does one grain look like?
good: Clear and shiny, like a tiny piece of glass.
A little box shape.

flow.do: 1. Now pour a small heap of sugar next to the single grains. 2. Compare. 3. Try the same with salt.
flow.say: One grain looks clear. So why does the heap look white?
flow.kid: Now look at a heap. Why does the heap look white?

ask.q: Why does the heap look white?
good: The light bounces off all the grains.
There are so many edges.

flow.parent: Salt grains are tiny clear cubes. Glass-making sand is made of tiny clear grains too, which is why melted sand can be clear.

activities.title: The Water Shake: paper or plastic?
activities.context: In this activity you shake a piece of tissue paper and a piece of plastic bag in jars of water. You see which one falls apart, and why.

materials.item: 2 jars or bottles with lids, half full of water
a piece of tissue paper or toilet paper, about the size of your palm
a piece of plastic carry bag, the same size
a steel plate

schedule.what: Put the tissue in one jar and the plastic in the other. Shake for 1 minute. Look. Pour each onto a plate.

activities.record: Draw what came out of each jar.

setup.art: Two jars of water side by side, one with a piece of white tissue, one with a piece of blue plastic bag.
setup.caption: 1. Put tissue in one jar and plastic in the other.

setup.art: A child shaking a closed jar hard.
setup.caption: 2. Close the lids and shake for 1 minute.

setup.art: A steel plate with soft white fluffy bits from the tissue, and beside it the plastic piece still whole.
setup.caption: 3. Pour each onto a plate and look.

flow.do: 1. Put the tissue in one jar and the plastic in the other. 2. Close the lids. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: What will happen to each one when we shake it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What will happen to each one when you shake it? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes each jar hard for 1 minute. 2. Hold the jars up to the light.
flow.say: Shake it hard! Now look. What happened to the tissue? What happened to the plastic?
flow.kid: Shake each jar hard. Count to 60. Now look.

flow.do: 1. Pour each jar onto the plate. 2. Pick up some of the tissue bits and feel them. 3. Read the card 'How paper is made from plants'.
flow.say: The tissue fell into tiny soft bits. These are plant fibres. Paper is made of them, pressed together. Why did the plastic stay whole?
flow.kid: Feel the soft bits. They are plant fibres. Why did the plastic stay whole?

ask.q: Why did the tissue come apart?
good: Water got between the fibres and they let go.
Paper is made of tiny threads stuck together.

flow.parent: Tissue falls apart fastest. Newspaper takes longer, so use tissue or toilet paper. Throw the mush in the dustbin, not down the sink.

activities.title: The Plastic Count: how many plastic things are in one room?
activities.context: In this activity you count the plastic things in one room, then find out which of them could be made from a natural material instead.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Pick one room. Make a tally mark for every plastic thing. Then circle the ones that could be made of a natural material.

activities.record: A tally chart of plastic things, with the ones that could be natural circled.

setup.art: A kitchen with a plastic bucket, a plastic water bottle, plastic containers and a plastic mug, each with a small star on it.
setup.caption: 1. Look around one room for plastic things.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list of things and tally marks beside it, some circled.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each one.

flow.do: 1. Pick one room, such as the kitchen or the bathroom. 2. Ask your child to guess how many plastic things are in it.
flow.say: How many plastic things do you think are in the kitchen? Guess a number.
flow.kid: Guess. How many plastic things are in this room?

flow.do: 1. Walk round the room together. 2. For every plastic thing, your child writes its name or draws it, and makes a tally mark. 3. Count the marks.
flow.say: Look on shelves and inside cupboards too. Every plastic thing gets a mark.
flow.kid: Find every plastic thing. Make a mark for each one. Count them.
flow.parent: Lids, packets, the handle of a knife and the switches on the wall all count.

flow.do: 1. Go down the list. 2. For each thing, ask if a natural material could do the job. 3. Circle those.
flow.say: Could this be made of wood, steel, clay, cloth or leaf instead? Which ones would be hard to replace?
flow.kid: Could it be wood, steel, clay or cloth instead? Circle those.

ask.q: Which plastic thing would be hardest to replace?
good: The bucket, because it must be light and not break.
The light switch, because it must keep electricity in.

games.title: Where Did It Start? A memory game
games.context: This is a memory card game. Each made thing has a partner card: the natural material it was made from. You find the pairs by turning over two cards at a time.

items.b: Made from: oil from under the ground
Made from: rock with iron in it

rules: Cut out all 20 cards. Mix them up. Lay them face down in rows.
The youngest player goes first. Turn over any two cards and read them aloud.
If one card is a thing and the other is what it was made from, you have a pair. Say how the start material was changed. Keep the pair and have another turn.
If they are not a pair, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
Check a pair by reading the back of the thing card.
When all the cards are gone, the player with the most pairs wins.

setup.art: Twenty small cards face down in four rows on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay all the cards face down.

setup.art: Two cards turned face up: 'A glass bottle' and 'Sand'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two. Is it a thing and its start material?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read all the pairs aloud once with your child. 3. Mix and lay them face down.
flow.say: Every made thing started as something natural. Let's read the pairs first, then hide them.
flow.kid: Read the pairs. Then mix them and turn them face down.

flow.do: Play until all the pairs are found. When a pair is found, the player says how the start material was changed.
flow.say: You found the bottle and the sand! How did the sand become a bottle?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Is it a pair? How was it changed?

ask.q: How did the sand become a bottle?
good: It was melted in a furnace and blown into a shape.
People heated it until it melted.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Ask one last question.
flow.say: Which start material was changed the most? Which was changed the least?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Which was changed the most?

check.why: Glass is made from melted sand. A notebook is made from a tree, and a plastic bucket from oil.

games.title: Stand Up, Sit Down: natural or made?
games.context: This is a moving game. A caller names a thing. Everyone stands up tall for a natural material and sits down for a material made by people.
rules: One player is the caller and holds the cards. Everyone else stands in a line.
The caller reads a card aloud, but not the back.
If it is a natural material, stand up tall. If it is made by people, sit down on the floor.
The caller reads the back. Anyone who got it wrong does 3 jumps and stays in.
If the back says 'Tricky', everyone stops. Each player says natural or made, and why. No one does jumps.
After 8 cards, a new player becomes the caller.

setup.art: Three children in a line, two standing tall and one sitting on the floor, with a girl holding cards in front of them.
setup.caption: 1. Stand in a line. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: A card reading 'A bird's nest' with a question mark.
setup.caption: 2. A tricky card: stop and talk.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Explain: stand for natural, sit for made.
flow.say: If nature made it, stand up tall. If people made it, sit down. Some cards are tricky.
flow.kid: Natural: stand up. Made by people: sit down.

flow.do: Play through the cards. When a tricky card comes, stop and let each player give a reason.
flow.say: A bird's nest. Is it natural or made? A bird made it from grass. People make paper from wood. What is the difference?
flow.kid: A bird's nest. Natural or made? Why?

ask.q: Is a bird's nest natural or made?
good: Natural, because a bird is part of nature.
Made, because the bird built it.
Both. The grass is natural, and the bird made the nest.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer to the tricky cards. Humans are animals too, so this is a real question.

flow.do: Ask one last question.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?

challenges.title: A Window for a Shoebox House
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Before glass was cheap, people in many places used other materials to let light into their homes. You make a window for a shoebox house without using glass.
challenges.problem: Cut a window in a shoebox. Cover it with a material that lets light in and keeps a puff of air or a sprinkle of water out. You must be able to tell a toy is inside without opening the box.
constraints: The window must be at least as big as a playing card.
materials: a shoebox or a carton with a lid
butter paper, a clear plastic packet, a polythene bag, a sheet of white paper, a few drops of cooking oil, cloth
general: A clear plastic packet taped over the hole.
Butter paper, which lets light in but blurs the view.
creative: White paper rubbed with a few drops of oil. The oil fills the gaps between the fibres, so more light gets through. Before glass was common, people in China and Japan used oiled paper or paper screens in windows.
A very thin slice of a clear plastic bottle, cut flat.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own window. Shine a torch through it from outside. Can you tell the toy is inside? Then make it better.

setup.art: A shoebox with a square window cut in one side and a toy elephant inside.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a window. Put a toy inside.

setup.art: A child rubbing a few drops of oil into a piece of white paper on a plate, with the oily patch looking see-through.
setup.caption: 2. Test window materials, like oiled paper.

setup.art: A torch shining through a paper window into the box, with the toy's shape just visible.
setup.caption: 3. Shine a torch in. Can you see the toy?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a window in the side of the box. 2. Your child puts a toy inside and closes the lid.
flow.say: Glass is a great window, because sand melted into one clear piece. What else could let light in?
flow.kid: Put a toy in the box. What could make a window, without glass?

flow.do: 1. Let your child try each material over the hole. 2. Rub a few drops of oil into a piece of white paper and try that too.
flow.say: Hold each one over the window. Which lets in the most light? Look at the oily paper. What changed?
flow.kid: Try each material. Which lets in the most light?

ask.q: Why does the oily paper let more light through?
good: The oil fills the gaps between the fibres.
It has fewer edges for the light to bounce off.

flow.parent: This is the same idea as the sugar test. Filling the gaps between fibres means less light bounces about.

flow.do: 1. Your child tapes the best material over the window. 2. Shine a torch through it from outside. 3. Sprinkle a few drops of water on it.
flow.say: Can you tell the toy is inside? Did the water get in?
flow.kid: Tape on your window. Shine a torch. Can you see the toy?

flow.do: Ask your child to change one thing and try again.
flow.say: What would make your window better?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Try again.

items.p: Sort these into natural materials and made materials.
items.why: Wood, clay and wool come from nature. Glass, plastic and paper are made by people from natural materials.

items.p: Draw a line from each made material to the natural material it is made from.
items.why: Every made material starts as a natural raw material.

items.p: In the sugar test, what did the sugar look like after it was melted and cooled?
items.why: Melted and cooled, the sugar set into one clear piece. Picking 'white grains' may mean thinking a material always keeps its look. Heat changed it.
items.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.

items.p: Draw the heap of sugar and the cooled sugar sheet, each on top of a word in the newspaper.
items.a: The heap hides the word. The word can be read through the sheet.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the word hidden under the heap and clear under the sheet.
items.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'heap' and 'sheet', each with a short printed word at the bottom.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the crushed sugar sheet look white?
items.a: Because it was in tiny pieces again, and light bounced off all their edges.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pieces have many edges, and light bounces off them.
items.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.

items.p: Paper is made from plants.
items.why: True. Paper is made of tiny plant fibres, from wood, bamboo or sugarcane waste, pressed together.

items.p: Bornali, a girl in Guwahati, counts plastic things in her bathroom. She finds a bucket, a mug, a soap box, a toothbrush and a comb. How many plastic things did she find?
items.why: Bucket, mug, soap box, toothbrush, comb: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
items.context: This question is about the plastic count, where you count all the plastic things in one room.

items.p: Three of these are natural. Which one is made by people?
items.why: A plastic bottle is made in a factory from oil. The others come straight from nature.

items.p: Label each picture with the natural material it was made from.
items.why: Each made thing started as a natural material.
items.art: Four small pictures with an empty label under each.

items.p: In the soil cup test, which piece changed the most in two weeks?
items.why: Bacteria and fungi in the soil eat banana peel quickly. Picking the plastic bag may mean mixing up 'changed most' and 'changed least'.
items.context: This question is about the soil cup test. You bury small pieces of banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a plastic bag in damp soil, and dig them up after one week and two weeks.

items.p: Kavya and her grandfather are choosing plates for a big family lunch at Onam.

views.says: Let's use banana leaves. They are natural, and they break down in the soil after.
Let's use our steel plates. They are made by people, but we wash them and use them for years.

items.ask: Whose plan would you pick? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason, such as 'the banana leaf broke down in the soil test'. It also says what the other is right about, such as 'steel plates are used again and again, so they make no rubbish'.
items.why: Both are good choices. One breaks down, the other lasts and is used again. Made does not always mean bad.

items.p: Arun, a boy of 5, says, 'Glass can't be made from sand. Sand is not clear.' What would you tell him? Use the sugar test.
items.a: The sugar heap was white too, but melted and cooled it became clear. Each grain lets light through, but a heap has many edges. Melted sand joins into one piece with no edges, so glass is clear.
items.why: A strong answer uses the sugar test as evidence, and says why melting makes the material clear.
items.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.

items.p: Why does glass-making need a furnace, not a stove?
opts: Sand needs much more heat to melt than sugar
items.why: Sugar syrup melts on a stove. Sand needs about 1,500 degrees Celsius, far hotter than any kitchen.

items.p: Put the steps of making paper in order.
items: Plant parts are cooked and beaten into a mush called pulp.
Wood, bamboo or sugarcane waste is collected.
The pulp is spread thin on a screen.
The sheet is pressed and dried.
items.why: First the plant parts are collected, then mashed into pulp, then spread thin, then pressed and dried.

items.p: Thara, a girl in Class 2, says, 'Plastic is not natural at all.' Is she right? What did plastic start as?
items.a: Partly. Plastic is made by people, but it starts as oil, which is natural. Oil formed long ago from tiny sea living beings.
items.why: A strong answer says plastic is a made material, and also names its natural raw material, oil.

items.p: Draw the journey of a glass bangle, from the beach to a wrist. Draw at least three steps.
items.a: Sand, then a furnace melting it, then a worker pulling or shaping hot glass, then a bangle on a wrist.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the sand is melted by heat, shaped while hot, and cooled.
items.art: A long empty box with three arrows across it.

items.p: The natural material that something is made from is called its ____ material.
items.why: Sand is the raw material for glass. Wood is a raw material for paper.

items.p: Clear glass, crushed into powder, would look white.
items.why: True. The powder has many tiny edges, and light bounces off all of them, just like the crushed sugar sheet.
items.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.

items.p: In the water shake, the tissue fell apart, but the plastic did not. Why?
opts: The tissue is made of fibres that let go of each other when wet
items.why: Paper is plant fibres holding each other. Water gets between them and they let go. Plastic is made of long chains that water does not pull apart.
items.context: This question is about the water shake. You shake a piece of tissue paper and a piece of plastic bag in a jar of water.

items.p: Meenakshi and her brother Farhan see a paper wasp's nest on their balcony.

views.says: The nest is natural. A wasp made it, and wasps are part of nature.
Then our notebooks are natural too. People are animals, and we made the paper the same way, from wood.

items.ask: Do you agree with Meenakshi, Farhan, or both? Give a reason. Then say one way a wasp's paper and our paper are different.
items.a: A strong answer gives a clear reason, for example that people are animals too, so both could be called natural. It also names a difference, for example that people use big machines, chemicals and factories.
items.why: There is no single right answer. It depends on where we draw the line between natural and made.

items.p: In the soil cup test, the plastic bag did not change in two weeks. Why could that be a problem if plastic is thrown on the ground?
items.a: Because it will stay there for a very long time. It does not break down like peel or paper, so it piles up.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test result and says what happens when plastic is not broken down.
items.context: This question is about the soil cup test. You bury small pieces of banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a plastic bag in damp soil, and dig them up after one week and two weeks.

videos.title: How glass is made in a glass factory
videos.why: Shows sand melting in a furnace and glowing glass being shaped, which a child cannot see at home.
videos.check: Find a real video showing a glass furnace and molten glass. Check the facts said before using it.

videos.title: Glass bangles being made in Firozabad
videos.why: Shows workers pulling and coiling hot glass into bangles, in India.
videos.check: Find a real video of bangle making in Firozabad. Watch it fully first.

videos.title: How paper is made from wood or bagasse
videos.why: Shows pulp being spread, pressed and dried into paper.
videos.check: Find a real video of a paper mill. Check the steps match the card.

quiz.p: Which of these is a natural material?
quiz.why: Cotton grows on the cotton plant. Glass and plastic are made by people. Picking glass may mean thinking anything clear and plain is natural.

quiz.p: Glass is made from which natural material?
quiz.why: Glass is made by melting sand in a furnace. Picking oil mixes it up with plastic.

quiz.p: Most plastic is made from what?
quiz.why: Plastic is made in factories from oil and natural gas. Picking melted sand mixes it up with glass.

quiz.p: Revathi, a girl in Kochi, watches her mother pour melted sugar onto a plate. When it cools, what will it look like?
quiz.why: In the sugar test, the melted sugar set into one clear piece. Picking 'white grains' means thinking it goes back to how it was.

quiz.p: Why does a heap of sugar look white?
opts: Light bounces off the edges of all the grains
quiz.why: Each grain lets light through, but a heap has thousands of edges that bounce light about. Picking 'painted white' means not yet having looked at one grain up close.

quiz.p: Why is a glass window clear, when sand is not?
opts: The sand melted into one piece with no edges inside
quiz.why: Melting joins all the grains into one piece. With no edges inside, light goes straight through.
Paper is made from wood, bamboo or sugarcane waste, mashed into fibres. In the water shake, the tissue fell apart into these fibres.

quiz.p: In the soil cup test, which piece did not change at all?
quiz.why: Soil bacteria and fungi have very few ways to eat plastic. Picking newspaper may mean thinking all made materials last. Paper is plant fibres, so it breaks down.

quiz.p: Selvi, a girl in Class 2, is not sure where a brick comes from. What is a brick made from?
quiz.why: Bricks are clay that is shaped and baked very hot. Melted sand makes glass, not bricks.

quiz.p: Before the sugar test, Farhan guessed the melted sugar would stay white. After the test, what should he do?
opts: Keep his guess, because guesses are always right
Say what he saw, and change his idea
Do the test again until it comes out white
quiz.why: A good scientist says what the test showed, even when it is different from the guess.

applications: Glass makers melt sand, and old crushed glass, to make bottles, windows, spectacles and bangles.
Paper mills in India make paper from wood, bamboo and sugarcane waste called bagasse.
Plastic factories make buckets, pipes, packets and polyester cloth from oil and gas.
Brick kilns bake clay into bricks for houses.
Recycling turns old glass, paper and plastic back into new things, so fewer raw materials are dug up or cut down.

spotted.text: Glass bangles stacked high at a stall before a festival. Many are made in Firozabad, in Uttar Pradesh.
spotted.art: A bangle stall with tall stacks of red, green and gold glass bangles, and a woman trying some on.

spotted.text: Banana leaves used as plates at a meal in Kerala or Tamil Nadu, then thrown on the compost.
spotted.art: A family eating rice and sambar on banana leaves.

spotted.text: A kabadiwala's cart with old newspapers, glass bottles and plastic, ready to be sold for recycling.
spotted.art: A man pushing a cart piled with bundled newspapers, bottles and plastic tins.

spotted.text: A potter in Kolkata's Kumartuli or in Puducherry shaping wet clay.
spotted.art: A woman potter shaping a pot on a turning wheel.

spotted.text: Coir mats and ropes made from coconut husk, sold in Kerala and in markets across India.
spotted.art: A stack of brown coir doormats and coils of coir rope at a shop.

open_questions.why_open: Glass is hard like a solid, but its particles are jumbled like a liquid's, not in neat rows. Physicists still argue about how best to explain what happens when melted glass goes hard.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last in soil and the sea?
open_questions.why_open: Plastic has only been made in large amounts for about 70 years. Nobody has watched a plastic bag for long enough to know when it is truly gone.

open_questions.q: Can we find tiny living beings that eat plastic quickly?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found a few bacteria and fungi that eat some kinds of plastic, but only slowly. They are still searching and testing.

ask_kids: What is your school bag made of? Is that natural or made by people?
If all the plastic in our home vanished, what would we miss most?
What natural material is your favourite? Why?
Look at the window. What do you think the glass was before it was glass?
Which things in our dustbin would break down in soil?

jokes.j: Why did the sand go to school?
jokes.a: It wanted to become a glass act!

jokes.j: What did the window say to the sand?
jokes.a: I can see right through you now!

jokes.j: Why did the notebook visit the forest?
What did the banana peel say to the plastic bag in the soil?
jokes.a: See you never, I'm breaking down!

jokes.j: Why was the glass bangle so calm?
jokes.a: It had already been through the fire.

jokes.j: What is a tree's favourite thing to read?
Why did the sugar grain feel shy in the heap?
jokes.a: Nobody could see through to the real her!

jokes.j: What did the clay say after the kiln?
jokes.a: I'm a brick now, and I'm not going back!

maths.problem: In the sugar test, Nila read 0 letters through the sugar heap and 8 letters through the sugar sheet. How many more letters could she read through the sheet?
maths.explain: 8 take away 0 is 8. The sheet showed 8 letters, the heap showed none.
maths.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.
maths.why_maths: Counting letters turns 'clearer' into a number, so we can compare the heap and the sheet.

maths.problem: The grown-up set a 10 minute timer for the sugar sheet to cool. After 4 minutes, Selvi asked if it was ready. How many more minutes did she have to wait?
maths.explain: Count on from 4 to 10: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. That is 6 minutes.
maths.context: This question is about the sugar test. A grown-up melts sugar with a little water and pours it on an oiled plate. When it cools, you compare it with a heap of dry sugar grains.
maths.why_maths: Working out the time left helps us wait safely until the hot sugar is hard.

maths.problem: Bornali counted 12 plastic things in her kitchen. Her friend Fathima counted 9 in hers. Who counted more, and how many more?
maths.explain: 12 is more than 9. Count on from 9 to 12: 10, 11, 12. That is 3.
maths.context: This question is about the plastic count, where you count all the plastic things in one room.
maths.why_maths: Comparing counts shows which home uses more plastic, and by how much.

maths.problem: In the changing line, Kavya put 8 things down. 5 were nearer the 'Changed a lot by people' end. How many were nearer the 'As nature made it' end? Which side had more?
maths.answer: 3 things. The 'changed a lot' side had 2 more.
maths.explain: 8 take away 5 is 3. 5 is more than 3, and 5 take away 3 is 2.
maths.context: This question is about the changing line. You lay things from home on a line, from 'as nature made it' to 'changed a lot by people'.
maths.why_maths: Counting each half tells us whether most of the things in our home were changed a lot by people.

maths.problem: In the soil cup test, Lakshmi waters each of her 4 cups with 2 spoons of water. How many spoons does she use every time she waters?
maths.context: This question is about the soil cup test. You bury small pieces of banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a plastic bag in damp soil, and dig them up after one week and two weeks.
maths.why_maths: Every cup gets the same water so the test is fair. Counting in twos tells us how much to fill.

roots.context: We have learnt that glass, paper and plastic are made from natural materials. Now we ask what the sugar test tells us about materials, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your heap of white sugar grains was not see-through. Melted and cooled, the same sugar set into a clear sheet. Each grain was already clear, but light bounced off all the edges between grains. Glass is clear because melting joins many sand grains into one piece with no edges inside.
deep_truth.habit: We think the colour of a material belongs to the material itself. The sugar was white as grains and clear as one piece, so how a material looks also depends on how its pieces meet.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sugar test, the dry heap hid the newspaper words, the cooled sheet showed them, and the crushed sheet turned white again. Single grains under a torch looked clear.

three.who_am_i: You are made of natural materials too: water, and things from the food you ate, which came from plants, soil and sun.
three.what_is_life: Living beings make materials. A cotton plant grows fibres, a silkworm spins silk, and a wasp chews wood into paper.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything people make, from a window to a bucket, began as sand, wood, clay, rock or oil from the Earth.

roots.thread: Sand, a glass bangle and the sea glass on a beach are all the same material, arranged in different ways. Heat joins the grains into one piece, and waves scratch them apart again. Everything is conscious, down to the particles in a grain of sand. The sand does not stop being itself when it becomes a bangle. It changes its shape and its place.

teachings.teaching: By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot and the lamp are only names and shapes. What is real is the clay.
teachings.link: A glass bottle, a window and a bangle have different names and shapes. Underneath, all three are melted sand.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper, and you can see the cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper.
teachings.link: Paper is made from a tree, and the tree grew from rain, soil and sunlight. A made material carries all of those natural things inside it.

science.text: Glass is a solid whose tiny particles are jumbled, not in neat rows. With no grain edges inside, light passes straight through.
Exactly what happens when a melted liquid sets into glass is still argued about by physicists.

other_view.view: They explain the clear sugar sheet only with light and tiny particles: light bounces off edges, and without edges it goes straight through. They do not use awareness to explain it.

practice.title: Look through the window
practice.say: Sit near a window. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. Look through the glass at the sky or the building across the road. This glass was once sand on a beach or a riverbank. Now it lets the light reach your eyes. Breathe in and out three more times, and keep looking.
practice.kid: Sit near a window. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out. Look through the glass. It was once sand. Breathe three more times.

ask: If glass is melted sand, is a window natural or made?
When sea glass turns back into sand, is it still glass?
What else might look one way in pieces and another way as one?
roots.art: A child sitting by a window, looking through the clear glass at the sky, with a faint picture of a sandy beach in the glass.

science: Glass manufacture: soda-lime glass is made from silica sand, soda ash and limestone, melted at about 1,500 degrees Celsius. Recycled glass (cullet) is added to the melt.
Granular materials look white because light scatters at the many surfaces between grains, while a single grain or a fused piece is transparent.
Sugar syrup at the hard crack stage (about 150 degrees Celsius) cools into a clear, brittle amorphous solid, used as 'sugar glass'.
Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 36: the story of merchants making glass with soda on a beach.

sources.walkthrough: The sugar test was thought through for a city kitchen. 4 tablespoons of sugar with 2 of water, boiled on a medium flame, reach the hard crack stage in about 6 to 10 minutes and turn pale gold. Poured as thin as a coin on an oiled steel plate, they set hard in about 10 minutes, clear enough to read newsprint through. Crushed in a cloth, the sheet turns to white powder. In humid weather the sheet goes sticky after some hours, so compare it soon after it cools. In the soil cup test, banana peel goes dark and soft within a week in damp soil, newspaper softens, cotton changes only a little in two weeks, and the plastic does not change.
